item.title: Extreme rainfalls flood Sri Lanka’s coastal city as wetlands, drains vanish
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- Several areas of Colombo, Sri Lanka’s commercial capital, were inundated following a high intensity downpour on Nov. 6, opening discussions on the city’s vulnerability to flash flooding.

- Sri Lanka is constrained by the lack of technology such as an operational Doppler weather radar system and hence cannot release accurate forecasts in time, according to weather officials.

- Despite being a RAMSAR-accredited wetland city, the water retention capacity of most wetlands in Colombo have declined due to urbanization, poor waste disposal and spread of invasive species.

- Economists suggest creating a dedicated financial reserve akin to an adaptation and resilience fund to enable local authorities to build resilient infrastructure.

COLOMBO — On Nov. 6, a 129-millimeter (5-inch) downpour flooded parts of Sri Lanka’s commercial capital within minutes, stranding commuters and submerging a large number of vehicles.

Siva Sivasagunthan, a three-wheeler driver working at a local ride-hailing app, told Mongabay that the water levels quickly increased and his vehicle was partially submerged in water. It took him around two hours to reach a location that would have usually taken 30 minutes to reach on a normal day. The downpour left many Colombo residents panicking.

According to Ajith Wijemanna, director of Sri Lanka’s Department of Meteorology, there have been a few instances over the decades when Colombo has experienced rainfall exceeding 400 mm (15.7 in). In June 1992, the city experienced a rainfall of 493.7 mm (19.4 in). In November 2010, a 440.2 mm (17.3 in) rainfall was recorded in 24 hours.

Wijemanna told Mongabay that the intensity of the rainfall — the speed of rainfall received in an hour — is extremely important. According to meteorological department readings, the rainfall intensity on Nov. 6 was more than 120 mm (4.7 in) per hour. The rain gauge reading at another location in Colombo indicated more than 135 mm (5.3 in) of rainfall per hour. “We believe that the main cause of flooding was the high intensity during a short period of time, such as an hour, which was similar to a gushing downpour,” Wijemanna said.

He noted that Sri Lanka currently lacked technology such as a Doppler radar system to support better forecasts with good lead time. Once the system is made fully operational, the agency will have the capacity to issue forecasts and predict rainfall with a lead time.

Pressure on an ancient drainage system

The flash flood occurred soon after Sri Lanka’s prime minister Harini Amarasuriya instructed officials in local authorities, including the department of irrigation and divisional secretariats, to clean canals and drainage systems in Colombo to ensure proper flow of rainwater. Following the flash flood, several authorities deployed workers to clean drains and canals and identified 60 key locations with blocked drains and waterways obstructing the flow of flood water.

According to Deepika Wijethilake, deputy director engineering of drainage design at the Colombo Municipal Council (CMC), the sewer and storm water systems in Colombo are about a century old and have been designed to function separately. She told Mongabay that the storm water system has been designed to withhold a capacity of 30 mm (1.18 in) of rainfall per hour.

“But on Nov. 6, there was a rainfall exceeding 100 mm [3.9 in] per hour. Since it rained heavily, there was extensive pressure on the system and it took some time for the water to recede,” she said, adding that the construction of more pavements also means less ability for rainwater absorption.

Real estate boom impacting wetlands

Besides grey infrastructure, Colombo’s wetlands also play a role in flood retention and mitigation. However, due to various development projects, Colombo’s wetlands are now under threat.

A 2025 study by the Colombo-based nonprofit Centre for a Smart Future (CSF) looked at the emerging environmental pressures from the booming real estate development in Colombo’s suburbs, particularly around the Thalangama environment protection area, a picturesque Colombo suburb. According to the study, wetlands, rice fields and peri-urban landscapes are being positioned as exclusive residential enclaves and marketed as ‘green living.’

The study showed that the desirable features of the wetlands were being highlighted by property developers to increase demand. Interestingly, it also referred to areas such as Kaduwela, Malabe and Thalawathugoda — areas considered residential and all situated around wetlands — having witnessed an annual spike in property prices by about 30-40%.

According to CSF co-founder and director Anushka Wijesinha, these property developers are doing very little to ensure what they market. “This is a very sensitive wetland complex. They are able to leverage on the wetland to create demand and price premia, but hardly ensure that their projects are nature-positive, which is problematic. The ecological value of the wetland is not reflected in the prices that are being charged or the fees paid to local councils or environmental authorities,” he told Mongabay.

Wijesinha said that most people see this green space idea narrowly and only from an aesthetic point of view. “But beyond that, it is a fundamental element of the city that makes the city resilient to various climate impacts. Over 45% of the country’s GDP is generated by the Western Province, of which Colombo is a major part. Then there’s a huge amount of logistics and international connectivity. There are supply chain risks when the city floods. Rather than concentrating on just the aesthetics, we need to look at it from a point of resilience, where these issues are a risk to the economic competitiveness of the city,” he said.

He highlighted the importance of assessing the economic worth of a wetland. Citing a 2003 study of the Muthurajawela wetland, a coastal peat bog near Colombo, Wijesinha said how this wetland complex provides certain ecosystem services such as flood control. “Without these services, the country would have to spend billions to put up [human]-made solutions,” he said.

Improving wetland connectivity

Colombo lies in a low-lying area downstream of the Kelani river basin and is a RAMSAR-accredited wetland city.

Chethika Gunasiri, an environmental scientist who focuses on urban wetlands and sustainability, noted that colonial cities are located in coastal or flood plain areas where floods are a natural phenomenon. “To mitigate these disasters, flood plain areas have natural infrastructure called wetlands. Their main function is to absorb rainwater, temporarily hold it and slowly release this water to the drainage system. Part of this water also goes through the soil and recharges the groundwater table,” she said.

The Colombo Wetland Complex (CWC) comprises several urban and municipal council areas and not only the Colombo Municipal Council area. According to Gunasiri, 37% of rainwater that comes into Colombo is retained by this wetland complex.

“But we now see how these wetlands are being filled and developed. The drainage system is not sufficient to manage high volumes of rainfall. There is no natural vegetation to retain or temporarily hold the water coming into the city,” she said.

According to her, around 20 square kilometers (7.7 square miles) of wetlands in the wetland complex remain, making it important to connect these wetlands to the Colombo flood management plan. “Most wetlands in Colombo are there as green patches, but their water retention capacity has decreased. Many wetlands have been invaded by pond apple [Annona glabra], [which has converted] them to terrestrial land where that water absorption capacity gets swiftly reduced. So we have to restore wetlands,” she said.

Sustainable solutions…

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-21 03:14 UTC

item.title: It’s time to put Africa’s forest communities on the map (commentary)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- The new standard world map adopted at the recent U.N. General Assembly more accurately depicts the size of Africa, which is in reality much larger than formerly standard Mercator projection maps.

- A new op-ed argues that there is now an urgent need for large-scale participatory mapping of community lands and resources in places like the Congo Basin — as well as accompanying legal and policy reforms to formally recognize these areas — as technologies and regional expertise now exist to put thousands of forest communities on the map.

- “A radically different and fairer vision of the Congo Basin is within grasp, and it starts with putting communities on the map,” the writers argue.

- This article is a commentary. The views expressed are those of the authors, not necessarily of Mongabay.

The U.N. General Assembly’s recent adoption of a new standard world map, more accurately reflecting the true size of Africa than depicted in the Eurocentric 16th-century Mercator projection, is great news and a welcome reminder that multilateralism isn’t dead yet.

It also doesn’t tell the whole story.

We’re not talking about how the continent was carved up between the former colonial powers through such events as the Berlin conference of 1884-1885, though the social, economic and political impacts of the often straight and artificial lines drawn on those maps are still felt today.

No, we’re talking about how maps of Central African states are still used by foreign interests and political elites as tools to perpetuate power — with control of natural resources and the benefits they generate tending to flow outwards and upwards — rather than to the people living in these areas.

Today, much of the Congo Basin, the world’s second largest rainforest, resembles a patchwork of extractive industry concessions, strictly protected areas and an ever-increasing array of carbon offset projects which our organization has documented. These have largely failed to stem deforestation and biodiversity loss, while delivering few or no benefits to local populations, and in many cases, causing severe impacts on human rights and food security.

What maps typically don’t show are the systems of longstanding customary rights and usage by Indigenous and local communities (IPLCs) that extend across the vast region, and which have been little documented, let alone formally recognized.

By our estimates, only around 5% of the forest is currently under formal community tenure or management rights, significantly less than the estimated 35% under Indigenous title in the Amazon despite a much higher population density. Most of these come in the form of community forests in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), while other countries in the region either have very ill-adapted legal frameworks for community tenure (Gabon or Cameroon) or no enforceable legislation at all (Central African Republic and Republic of Congo).

The continued absence of forest community tenure from maps is not only deeply socially unjust, but it also goes against the evidence that the best and fairest way to protect forests is to place them under the formal control of the people who live there. Lack of tenure clarity and security is also one of the biggest impediments to self-determination and responsible investment in the region, including a new wave of payment for environmental service schemes planned in the region.

So, what needs to happen? First, governments and donors in the region need to accelerate and implement legal and policy reforms related to community land tenure.

Encouragingly, several important steps have recently been taken in this direction. Last November at the climate COP in Belem, Brazil, the DRC government committed to placing more than 50 million hectares (over 123 million acres) under the control of IPLCs, a tenfold increase on the current area, alongside other reforms it is advancing on Indigenous rights and land-use planning. Other positive examples include draft legislation on community forests in the Central African Republic and on community managed protected areas in Gabon and Cameroon.

These are all promising developments, but laws are only powerful insofar as they are enforceable. To turn these commitments into tangible and enforceable tenure rights for forest-dwelling communities, there is an urgent need to scale up demarcation and recognition of these areas.

That is why the second key need is to greatly expand provision for participatory mapping tools and support, so that communities themselves can demonstrate their presence in the forest and for policy makers and the private sector to take account of and recognize this presence.

Our MappingForRights program has supported hundreds of communities in the Congo Basin to produce highly accurate and detailed maps of their resources and territories, but this covers only a fraction of what is needed.

Thankfully, advances in mapping technologies are breaking down cost barriers and making it easier for communities to generate, control and manage their data and to integrate this into government cadasters. There is also a large pool of untapped civil society capacity in the region to facilitate participatory mapping processes.

The challenge now is to bring all this altogether and make these resources widely available to forest peoples and grassroots organizations across the region, to enable the vital mapping of thousands of ‘invisible’ communities and to turn promising laws and policies into enforceable rights.

A radically different and fairer vision of the Congo Basin is within grasp, and it starts with putting communities on the map.

Georges Thierry Handja is senior manager of the Land and Livelihoods program for Rainforest Foundation UK, where Joe Eisen is executive director.

Banner image: New technologies paired with regional expertise can help put thousands of forest communities on the map of Africa. Image courtesy of Cargill.

item.title: Where family foundations can help marine conservation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- Research and reporting from across the Americas show that marine conservation outcomes depend heavily on how well protected areas are managed, fishing regulations are enforced, and local communities are involved in decision-making.

- Some of the most promising opportunities for smaller family foundations lie in improving the management of existing marine protected areas, strengthening community fishing rights, and addressing shortcomings in illegal fishing enforcement.

- The evidence for habitat restoration is more mixed, while research on migratory marine species points to opportunities to improve fisheries management beyond the boundaries of protected areas.

- Drawing on academic literature and Mongabay’s reporting in English, Spanish, and Portuguese, Founder Founder and CEO Rhett Ayers Butler examines where relatively modest philanthropic investments could help address persistent gaps in marine conservation.

COP17 ended in Armenia amid disappointment over the lack of concrete measures to reduce biodiversity loss by 2030. Finance was a sore point. Philanthropy is only a small part of that picture, but foundations can take risks that public agencies often cannot. I think there are some particularly good opportunities for smaller foundations in marine conservation.

My intended audience is family foundations that give away perhaps $2 million to $15 million a year and have a handful of staff.

Over the summer I went through the academic literature and Mongabay’s coverage in English, Spanish, and Portuguese to see what the evidence actually shows about marine conservation outcomes in the Americas. A first summary of that assessment – “From paper parks to lasting protection, here’s what works in marine conservation” – appeared last month. In some cases Mongabay’s reporting helped me understand why the results of a study were so disappointing. Our reporters had spoken to the people responsible for managing these areas, as well as people who lived or fished in them.

In reading about some of these places, I was struck by how long the laws protecting them had been on the books. Some of the agencies responsible for enforcing those laws lack adequate funding. Elsewhere, the designation of a protected area was done with little regard for the people who fished there.

Making existing protected areas work

I suspect it’s easier to raise money to establish a marine protected area (MPA) than to pay the salaries of the people who will patrol it. The same applies to restoration: there is often more interest in planting mangroves than in what happens to those mangroves three or four years later.

No-take reserves and other highly protected areas have a strong ecological track record. But even some of the better-known MPAs in the Americas have problems with illegal fishing. At Revillagigedo, the Mexican archipelago in the Pacific, Mongabay found that some complaints of illegal fishing had been archived or remained unresolved.

Some MPAs have been in existence for years without the ecological monitoring needed to determine whether they’re working. There are others where I think money would be better spent on enforcing fishing restrictions or working with local fishers.

If the agency responsible for an MPA lacks the legal authority to enforce its rules, better-equipped patrols may accomplish very little. And if a grant is going to pay for patrols, who will pay for them once the grant runs out?

Fishing rights and local governance

Some of the more interesting opportunities involve relatively small fishing communities. These communities don’t necessarily need an MPA to manage the waters they fish. Chile’s territorial use rights for fisheries (TURFs) and fisher-created refuges show how area-based rights and local organization can support stewardship. Costa Rica’s marine areas for responsible fishing may do more for conservation than standard protected-area figures suggest.

Getting legal recognition for an area that fishers already manage could be a good use of a foundation’s money. So could helping a fisher organization keep better records of what its members are catching.

I’d want to know who actually makes decisions about the fishery. Women and poorer fishers may have little say, even in places heralded for community-led conservation. And sometimes it’s an outside organization that has most of the authority.

Enforcing fishing regulations

Illegal fishing is much easier to detect than it used to be, but seeing a boat on a screen is a long way from boarding it or levying fines on its owner.

At Revillagigedo, patrolling a vast marine reserve more than 500 kilometers off Mexico’s Baja California is difficult and costly. Before funding more surveillance at Revillagigedo, I’d want to know why some of the cases mentioned in our reporting didn’t go anywhere. Was it a problem with the evidence or with what the authorities did with it?

It may be considerably cheaper to catch a vessel breaking the law when it comes into port than when it’s hundreds of kilometers out at sea.

I’d be particularly mindful of the risks of asking local people to document illegal fishing in areas where the boats belong to powerful commercial or political interests.

Restoring coastal habitats

I was less convinced by some of what I read about restoration. Restoration projects appeal to funders partly because planting is easy to count. But the number of seedlings or coral fragments says little about whether a damaged habitat will recover. In mangrove restoration, for example, reestablishing tidal flow may be more important than planting trees. On reefs, the conditions that contributed to the loss of corals, including pollution and overfishing, may need to be addressed before much is spent on outplanting.

In Florianópolis, in southern Brazil, one of the arguments for restoring mangroves is the protection they afford coastal communities as the climate changes. Some of the money for this work could potentially come from climate funders.

Beyond protected areas

I spent some time looking at conservation efforts in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, particularly in the waters around Galápagos, Cocos, Coiba, Malpelo and Gorgona (CMAR). These islands are important for some of the same populations of migratory marine animals.

Much has been made of the marine corridors in this part of the Pacific. Research on shark movements helped make the case for the creation of Ecuador’s Hermandad Marine Reserve in 2022. But a study published this year found that silky sharks tagged in Galápagos spent about half their time outside protected areas. Could seasonal fishing restrictions or changes in fishing gear reduce shark mortality there? That seems worth exploring.

Even where MPAs have benefited from decades of investment, fisheries management can remain a problem. Conservation groups have worked on the Mesoamerican Reef for decades, and Belize has long-term monitoring and ways of financing its MPAs. Overfishing is still widespread, and most commercial stocks still lack catch controls.

Sharks, rays, turtles, seabirds and forage fish die in fisheries operating well beyond the boundaries of protected areas. Studies of illuminated gillnets in Peru have shown that bycatch can be reduced while maintaining target catch and market value.

On the demand side, Mongabay has reported on government purchases of shark meat in Brazil and the mislabeling of shark meat in Ecuador. I wouldn’t know where to begin as a small funder interested in addressing either problem without the help of someone who knows the industry well.

One question I had while reading some of the studies was what happened after the researchers left. Was there still money to manage the protected area or maintain the restoration site five years later?

There may be some good opportunities to provide a few years of funding to MPAs that are in the process of securing government funding or setting up a trust fund.…

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-20 17:48 UTC

Original link: https://news.mongabay.com/2026/11/where-family-foundations-can-help-marine-conservation/

item.title: Ecuador copper mine advancing despite opposition from Indigenous communities
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- The Warintza copper mine in southeastern Ecuador could force Indigenous Shuar communities to relocate, while clearing primary forest and altering natural waterways.

- The mine would operate within the Indigenous territory, overlapping with a stretch of the Andes mountains known as the Cordillera del Cóndor.

- Critics of the project say the government granted exploration rights without consulting the communities.

- Now, the government is conducting another consultation. However, many residents say they no longer trust the process and believe the project will move forward regardless of their objections.

A proposed copper mine on Indigenous land in southeastern Ecuador is getting closer to opening despite opposition from some Shuar communities, who say they reject the project altogether and don’t want to participate in talks with the government.

The Warintza mine received environmental authorization this year, and officials will now begin meeting with Indigenous communities about how the project, if constructed, would impact their way of life. But some community members don’t want to be consulted at all, and say they’re worried about relocation from the territory.

“We want absolutely nothing to do with mining,” one community member, who asked to remain anonymous due to fear for his personal safety, told Mongabay. “And we don’t even want to be consulted.”

If the project moves forward, Lowell Mineral Exploration Ecuador S.A., a subsidiary of Solaris Resources, would extract copper for around 22 years from approximately 8,660 hectares (21,399 acres) across six concessions. It would also extract molybdenum concentrates and some gold and silver.

Construction would clear more than 2,025 hectares (5,003 acres) of primary forest and divert the Warints and Piuntz rivers, critical to Indigenous communities’ way of life, according to the environmental impact assessment, which received technical approval in April.

It could irreversibly change the landscape in some places even after the mine is closed, the assessment said. Surface water and groundwater quality also face high risk, threatening aquatic flora and fauna.

The area sits in the Cordillera del Cóndor, a stretch of the Andes that extends into Peru. The mine site provides habitat for 552 plant species, 20 of them endemic, according to the assessment. It also has 154 bird species, 69 amphibians and reptiles, and 31 mammal species, including the Andean bear (Tremarctos ornatus).

One activist, who wished to remain anonymous due to fear for his personal safety, told Mongabay the assessment left out other threatened and endangered species, and disregarded some pollution risks.

“There are serious errors regarding the types of chemicals that will be emitted, the heavy metals and the radioactive metals that will come out of the mine,” he said.

Solaris Resources didn’t respond to a request for comment from Mongabay in time for publication.

The mine would also overlap with homes in the Shuar communities of Warints and Yawi, the assessment said. The open pit would be around 3.4 kilometers (2.1 miles) long and 1.2 kilometers (0.75 miles) wide, and a tailings facility would cover around 860 hectares (2,125 acres).

The operations are so close to the villages that it would be unsafe for them to stay, the assessment said. It recommended total relocation of residents, approximately 512 Warints people and 210 Yawi. It rejected “scattered individual relocation” and moving into nearby mestizo communities as options.

“The impact cannot be avoided or minimized through design adjustments, so relocation is unavoidable, and planned relocation is an enabling condition for eliminating exposure and serious risk,” the assessment said.

Relocation is first subject to Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), a process in which communities are given the nature, size, pace, reversibility and scope of the project and how it could impact their lives.

In 2021, a complaint with the International Labour Organization (ILO), a U.N. agency, argued that Ecuador should have begun that process before granting the company exploration rights in the area. In 2024, the ILO upheld that position and also said the mine shouldn’t move forward without consulting the Shuar communities of Maikiuants, Warints, Yawi and Tinkimints.

In a September statement, Solaris Resources said it’s working toward finalizing water permits, mining concession administrative processes, infrastructure-related clearances and other legal requirements.

It also said the Warints and Yawi communities had finalized “life plans,” defined as community-led, long-term development frameworks that identify each community’s priorities and aspirations and provide a roadmap for future decision-making.

Company agreements with communities don’t qualify as consultation, the 2024 ILO ruling noted.

The Ministry of Energy and Mines didn’t respond to Mongabay’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Some residents say they’ve lost confidence in the consultation process after the exploration rights were granted without consultation in 2021. They said they’re worried the government will authorize the project regardless of what the communities decide.

“The government violates [our] constitutional rights and the international rights reinforcing them. Nevertheless, after all of that, they want to hold a prior and well-informed consultation,” the same community member told Mongabay.

If the communities ultimately reject the process, the project can still legally move forward. Ministry of Energy and Mines regulations say consultation results are non-binding, and the state can proceed without consent if it makes efforts to minimize impact and fairly compensate residents.

“It’s no longer a consultation process,” the activist said, “but instead becomes a process of negotiation and harm.”

Banner image: The outside of a traditional Shaur kitchen. Image by Brandi Morin/Survival International.

item.title: Could a short tail mean a new monkey species in Laos? Some scientists think so
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- A new-to-science species of monkey has recently been proposed in the Vietnamese Journal of Primatology: the short-tailed langur, or Trachypithecus brevicaudus.

- The description is based on analysis of photographs of monkeys in the Annamite Mountains of Laos with unusually short tales.

- Although other new-to-science primate species have initially been described on the basis of photographs, an independent expert interviewed by Mongabay says he doesn’t believe the data yet support the declaration of a distinct langur species.

- The next stage for the researchers is to collect droppings to use in genetic analysis, and to search for remains in nearby villages.

There is no body. No genetic evidence — yet. There are just photos, but some scientists say those photos show a distinct enough primate to declare it a new species: the short-tailed langur, or Trachypithecus brevicaudus. The proposed species was described in the Vietnamese Journal of Primatology and lives in the Annamite Mountains of Laos.

“A photograph of a langur, published by the Saola Foundation, caught my attention because the animal’s tail is noticeably shorter than that of any other species within this group of limestone langurs,” said Tilo Nadler, lead author of the paper and a wildlife consultant for the Vietnamese government and various NGOs.

This photo led Nadler and colleagues to investigate. They traveled to the area, a remote set of limestone karsts in Bolikhamxai province in central Laos, and took their own photos.

“The first time I observed a group of these langurs, it was immediately clear to me that they were different from all the other limestone langurs I had previously encountered and knew well,” Nadler told Mongabay in an email interview. “It was a very exciting experience.”

But not all scientists agree that these photos prove a new-to-science species.

“It could well be a new species, but I think the data that have been presented do not give sufficient support for this,” said primate expert Vincent Nijman, director of EcoVerde Global Consulting, who wasn’t involved with the paper.

But Nadler said the encounter, and photos, proved his hunch: this wasn’t a one-off case of an animal that lost part of its tail, but a whole population of langurs with shorter, thicker tails. To the untrained eye, the tail of the short-tailed langur still looks quite long, but it’s noticeably shorter than other related species, according to Nadler. (Hence the proposed name: brevicaudus means “short tail.”)

“These animals possess a shorter and thicker tail compared to closely related species of limestone langurs from the southern group — such as the Lao langur (Trachypithecus laotum) and the Hatinh langur (T. hatinhensis),” Nadler wrote.

He added he tried to scour local villages for any specimens that may have been hunted, to take back for genetic testing, but was unable to find any remains.

A future expedition plans to search for remains more thoroughly in local villages and collect the monkey’s droppings to use in genetic analysis.

Nadler said he’s not the first scientist to describe a new primates based only on photos: the highland mangabey (Rungwecebus kipunji) from Tanzania in 2003, and the Arunachal macaque (Macaca munzala) in 2005, and white-cheeked macaque (Macaca leucogenys) in 2015, both from the Himalayas, were all first described from just photos, with DNA to come later.

Nijman agreed that a species can be described using just photos and based on a single characteristic — in this case the tail. But he said he’s not convinced by the paper’s findings, arguing that the tail measurements as currently done still show some potential overlap with other species.

“The Hatinh langurs (male and female) with the shortest tails have as short a tail as the new species with the longest tail,” Nijman said via email. As for thickness, “they were not able to quantify this,” Nijman wrote.

Whether a new species or not, it was first photographed by Rob Timmins, the technical director of the Saola Foundation, in 2024. The Saola Foundation is currently searching for the saola (Pseudoryx nghetinhensis), a species of bovid often called the Asian unicorn, in the Annamite Mountains.

Lorraine Scotson, CEO of the Saola Foundation for the Conservation of the Annamite Mountains, said in an email interview that the group wasn’t involved with Nadler’s research, but that “a new primate is significant news, and we’d love to see this species get the wide attention it deserves.”

The Annamite Mountains are a biodiversity hotspot, housing dozens of species found nowhere else, including the giant muntjac (Muntiacus vuquangensis), the Annamite striped rabbit (Nesolagus timminsi), two species of gibbon, and the Laotian rock rat, or kha-nyou (Laonastes aenigmamus). Three percent of the world’s land-based vertebrates are found in the Annamite Mountains, which likely hosts many undescribed species.

Not long ago, the karst-dwelling monkey was the victim of heavy hunting, Nadler said.

“In the past, these langurs were hunted extensively, particularly in connection with the cultivation of hidden poppy fields used for opium production,” he said. “However, poppy cultivation has ceased due to legislation and strict enforcement, and with it, the hunting has also come to an end.”

Still, many mysteries remain. Chief among them: how many short-tailed langurs are there? Nadler said their range is “unclear,” with only two populations currently known. But he added, “there are other, extremely inaccessible limestone massifs where further populations might exist.”

Next year, the Saola Foundation plans to launch a new program with this proposed new species as its flagship animal to conserve these unique limestone karsts.

“Having been geographically isolated for millions of years, this karst complex habitat is likely to host many other endemic species of the Annamites Bioregion,” Scotson said, “and quite possibly some of them still undescribed to science.”

Banner image: A group of short-tailed langurs consisting of five adults (three in the photo) and two juveniles, approximately 1.5 to 2 years old. Image by Tilo Nadler.

item.title: Quechua community in Peru builds up Andean bear camera trap project on their own reserve
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- An Indigenous-led conservation project on the Pumataki private community reserve in Peru, gathers data on the presence and numbers of Andean bears — compiling some of the first local records of the species on the reserve.

- The project was developed by Maribel Pacco, a local from the Pillco Grande community, who uses the camera traps to inform a Quechua-language environmental education program for youth, though limited funding has forced the project to scale back some of its future plans.

- Pumataki is recognized by a legal framework which allows landowners, in this case the community of Pillco Grande, to convert their holdings into a nature reserve called a Private Conservation Areas (ACP).

- The Andean bear (Tremarctos ornatus) is listed as vulnerable to extinction on the IUCN Red List; in Peru, it is threatened by habitat loss, poaching and the impacts of climate change.

Maribel Pacco grins as she recalls the first time she saw an Andean bear close-up in the wild. At the forest edge, a mother and her cubs browsed on bromeliads while the volunteer ranger watched for hours in awe.

“I’m not a biologist, but at that moment, I decided to become a conservationist,” she says.

Today, Pacco leads a camera-trap project to estimate bear numbers and movements in Pumataki, a private community-owned reserve in the buffer zone of Manu National Park, in southeastern Peru. With the help of her Indigenous Quechua community of Pillco Grande, the project has generated some of the first local records of Andean bears (Tremarctos ornatus) in Pumataki. So far, they have identified 10 individual Andean bears, distinguishable by the unique pattern of facial markings.

Though modest and only 3 years old, information gathered from the camera traps helps inform a Quechua-language environmental education program for youth and is shared at community meetings to highlight the area’s biodiversity.

“In the last few years, I’ve seen a lot more involvement of women in Andean bear conservation which is fantastic to see,” said Rebecca Zug, a professor of biology at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito, who is not involved in the project. “There is also so much more power in Indigenous communities building conservation from within and learning about their own biodiversity from someone like Maribel than in having an outside voice come in.”

For now, limited funding has forced the project to scale back some of its future plans. However, environmental education and camera trap monitoring continue, with community members taking turns in groups of five to visit the reserve and to maintain the cameras.

The team Pacco has gathered is analyzing the behavior and activity patterns of different species to compile a biodiversity inventory. They hope the information gathered on the number of Andean bears and their territories will be used by universities in future research.

The Andean bear, also known as the spectacled bear, roams from Venezuela and Colombia in the north to northern Argentina in the south while facing an array of threats along the way. Despite being classified as vulnerable on the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, Andean bear populations face pressures from habitat loss and fragmentation, poaching, retaliatory killings due to crop raiding and the effects of climate change.

Peru, particularly in southeastern Peru where Pumataki is located, is one of the species’ strongholds. An estimated 5,000 bears are believed to roam cloud forests, dry forests, and the páramo and puna grasslands across the country.

“Peru has some of the biggest blocks of habitat left for the species across its range, but this is a forest-dependent species, so habitat loss and habitat fragmentation are major threats,” says Russ Van Horn of the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and co-chair of the IUCN Andean Bear Expert Team.

Important refuges remain where extensive protected forests continue to support Andean bear populations. Pumataki — a private cloud forest reserve — is one such refuge in the Cusco region.

Bridging different communities

Though small in size, this reserve is recognized by a legal framework which allows landowners to convert their holdings into a nature reserve called a Private Conservation Areas (ACP). Recognition can be granted for a minimum of 10 years, with the possibility of renewal, or made in perpetuity.

Pumataki lies on the eastern slopes of the Andes, bordering the vast Manu National Park. Often shrouded in mist, the forest teems with wildlife. It is a home to the Indigenous Quechua community of Pillco Grande, whose members own and manage the reserve.

For local people, this rugged landscape traditionally holds deep spiritual significance. It is the abode of Apu Kañaqway, a sacred mountain revered in the Quechua worldview as a protective spirit.

For Pacco, who grew up among these forests, conservation is entwined with a spiritual connection to the land.

“In my childhood, I would hear stories about the Apu, which is very important in our culture, and my father would take me to visit the reserve where he worked as a volunteer guard,” she says.

Pacco’s early connection to the landscape eventually drew her into conservation work. During college, she became a volunteer ranger in Manu National Park, where she encountered one of its most elusive residents: The Andean bear. She quickly developed a fascination with the species, she tells Mongabay.

“I fell in love with bears, their behavior, everything about them, and the role they play in the forest ecosystem. The other rangers taught me how to track their footprints and use camera traps, and I learned a lot,” she says.

Those experiences laid the foundation for her own conservation project. In 2023, Pacco received a Conservamos por Naturaleza (We Conserve for Nature) grant from the Peruvian Society for Environmental Law (SPDA) to launch a community-led initiative to monitor Andean bears in Pumataki and conduct environmental education.

According to the SPDA, Pacco’s ability to bridge different communities was a strength.

“Maribel can connect with different people. She speaks Quechua and can communicate with local communities, but she also speaks Spanish and English and can communicate with people from abroad,” says Carolina Butrich, a manager at the SPDA.

A community effort

Tracking one of the cloud forest’s most elusive large mammals is no easy feat. With camera traps, a GPS device and training from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Pacco began surveying the forest and reaching out to her community to document the presence of bears.

One of the principal hurdles, however, was getting more local people to participate.

“The biggest challenges were getting more people in the community involved, because most of us are just looking for ways to work and support our families,” says Justa Peña Condori, an early recruit to the team.

Gradually, through persistence and group meetings, Pacco was able to convince more community members to accompany her on camera-trapping excursions in the forest. She also began conducting environmental education in Quechua at the local school, teaching children about Andean bear ecology using images and video footage captured by the camera traps.

Individual bears can be distinguished by their own “fingerprint”: A unique pattern of facial markings around the eyes, often resembling spectacles. These markings allow the team to identify individual bears caught on camera. The process has also been a way to engage schoolchildren, who can give each bear a name and learn about conservation in a more personal way.

The camera traps have so far identified 10 individual Andean bears, providing the first records of the species in the area. The traps have also caught images of other cloud forest species such as the clouded oncilla (Leopardus pardinoides), dwarf brocket deer (Subulo chunyi), puma (Puma concolor), opossums and coatis helping to shift local attitudes toward wildlife.…
